prompt: What happens to a message in a queue once its consumer acknowledges it?

choices.text: It is deleted
choices.why: Right. The queue's length is the work still to do.

choices.text: It moves to the end of the queue for the next consumer
choices.why: That would hand finished work out again.

choices.text: It stays, and the consumer's offset moves past it
choices.why: That is a log; a queue keeps no offset.

choices.text: It is copied to every other consumer of the queue
choices.why: Competing consumers each get different messages.

prompt: A new loyalty system wants last month's sales. Where can it get them, if Ponto Final had put them on a RabbitMQ queue instead of Kafka?

choices.text: From the queue, by rewinding to the start of the month
choices.why: A queue has no offset to rewind.

choices.text: From a fanout exchange bound to a new queue
choices.why: A new queue receives only what is published from now on.

choices.text: Not from the broker: acknowledged messages were deleted
choices.why: Right. A queue has no replay.

choices.text: From the dead-letter queue, which keeps a copy of every message
choices.why: It keeps only what was given up on.

prompt: A fourth packer is added during the busiest hour. What does a queue do that a Kafka topic with three partitions and three consumers would not?

choices.text: Gives it work at once, with nothing to plan
choices.why: Right. In the group, a fourth member past three partitions sits idle (lesson 4).

choices.text: Rebalances the partitions so all four get a share of the existing ones
choices.why: That is what Kafka tries, and with three partitions one member gets none.

choices.text: Copies every order to the new packer too, so it can catch up on what the others did
choices.why: Competing consumers never get the same message.

choices.text: Doubles the throughput of the other three
choices.why: It adds one packer's capacity, nothing more.

prompt: Why does the lesson call moto an emulator?

choices.text: It is AWS's official local edition of SQS and SNS, maintained by Amazon
choices.why: It is an independent library, not Amazon's.

choices.text: It imitates AWS's APIs; its timings and limits are its own
choices.why: Right. Nothing measured against it says anything about Amazon's service.

choices.text: It forwards each request to AWS with fake keys
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson talks to AWS.

choices.text: It runs RabbitMQ under SQS names
choices.why: It is its own Python implementation.

prompt: pika connects to RabbitMQ as `guest`. Why is that acceptable in this lab and not on a shared server?

choices.text: `guest` has no password, and the lab has no network
choices.why: Its password is `guest`, and the restriction is about where it connects from.

choices.text: `guest` is read-only
choices.why: It can publish and consume, as the programs do.

choices.text: `guest` connects only from localhost, its whole protection
choices.why: Right. A reachable server gets its own users and deletes guest.

choices.text: pika encrypts the password
choices.why: The point is who can reach the server, not encryption.

prompt: A program publishes to the exchange `""` with routing key `packing`. Where does the message go?

choices.text: Nowhere, because the exchange has no name
choices.why: The empty name is the default exchange, which exists.

choices.text: To every queue on the server
choices.why: That would be a fanout, and only to bound queues.

choices.text: To the queue named `packing`
choices.why: Right. The default exchange routes by queue name.

choices.text: To a new queue that RabbitMQ creates with a random name
choices.why: The default exchange never creates queues.

prompt: Bia packed `web-0004` and crashed before `basic_ack`. What happened to the order?

choices.text: It was lost with her process
choices.why: The server still held it as unacknowledged.

choices.text: Ana received it, marked redelivered, and it was packed twice
choices.why: Right. At-least-once: nothing lost, something done twice.

choices.text: It waited on the server until Bia's process came back to finish it
choices.why: The server gives it to any consumer once the connection closes.

choices.text: It went to the dead-letter queue
choices.why: A crash is not a rejection; it went back on the queue.

prompt: What does `basic_qos(prefetch_count=1)` change for a slow packer?

choices.text: It holds at most one unacknowledged order at a time
choices.why: Right. The rest stay free for whoever is idle.

choices.text: It makes the server wait one second between deliveries to it
choices.why: It limits how many are outstanding, not the pace.

choices.text: It acknowledges each message automatically after one second
choices.why: Acknowledging is still the program's job.

choices.text: It lets only one packer connect to the queue
choices.why: Ana and Bia were both connected.

prompt: A queue is declared `durable=True`, but the messages are published without a persistent delivery mode. The server restarts. What is in the queue?

choices.text: All the messages, because the queue is durable
choices.why: Durability of the queue covers the queue, not its messages.

choices.text: Nothing, and the queue itself is gone too
choices.why: The durable queue comes back.

choices.text: Only the messages that had been acknowledged before the restart
choices.why: Acknowledged messages were already deleted.

choices.text: The queue, empty
choices.why: Right. RabbitMQ needs both: a durable queue and persistent messages.

prompt: Match each exchange type to when a bound queue gets the message.

pairs.right: the binding key equals the routing key
the binding pattern matches the routing key word by word

right_distractors: only when the queue has no consumer

prompt: In `rabbit_routes.py`, how many of the queues bound to `pf.topic` received `sale.recife`?
`natal` was published to the direct exchange, and no binding said `natal`. What happened?

choices.text: It waited in the exchange until a matching queue was bound
choices.why: Exchanges store nothing.

choices.text: It was dropped, and the publisher was not told
choices.why: Right. `mandatory=True` and publisher confirms are how a producer finds out.

choices.text: It went to `recife-only`, the only queue bound to that exchange
choices.why: A direct exchange compares keys; `natal` is not `recife`.

choices.text: `basic_publish` raised an exception
choices.why: It returned normally; that is the trap.

prompt: In a topic exchange, the binding pattern `*.recife` matches `refund.recife` because `*` stands for exactly one ___.
A packer rejects a message with `requeue=False` on a queue that has a dead-letter exchange. Where does the message go?

choices.text: Back to the front of the same queue
choices.why: That is `requeue=True`, and the endless loop.

choices.text: Republished, marked `rejected`, to be collected elsewhere
choices.why: Right. And a queue bound there collects it.

choices.text: It is deleted, as an acknowledgement would delete it
choices.why: Without a dead-letter exchange it would be; with one, it is republished.

choices.text: To the other consumers, one copy each
choices.why: Nothing in a queue is copied to several consumers.

prompt: Match each `x-death` reason to what happened to the message.

pairs.right: a consumer rejected it without requeueing
it waited longer than its TTL
the queue was full and it was the oldest

prompt: Orders on a packing queue are given a TTL of ten minutes with no dead-letter exchange. What goes wrong on the busiest day?

choices.text: The queue refuses new orders after ten minutes of backlog
choices.why: A TTL expires messages; it does not refuse them.

choices.text: The orders are redelivered every ten minutes to a different packer
choices.why: Expiry removes; it does not redeliver.

choices.text: Orders that wait too long are deleted, quietly
choices.why: Right. An order that waited still has to be packed.

choices.text: Nothing: TTL only applies to unacknowledged messages
choices.why: It applies to messages waiting in the queue.

prompt: An SQS consumer receives a message and crashes without deleting it. When can another consumer receive it?

choices.text: At once, because the connection closed
choices.why: SQS has no connection to watch; it uses a clock.

choices.text: After the visibility timeout
choices.why: Right. In the demo, nothing at once and the message again after 6 seconds.

choices.text: Never: an SQS message is delivered exactly once
choices.why: A standard queue is at-least-once.

choices.text: When an operator moves it back by hand
choices.why: It comes back by itself.

prompt: Packing an order takes 40 seconds and the queue's visibility timeout is 30. Nothing crashes. What do you see?

choices.text: Every order processed twice
choices.why: Right. The message reappears while the first packer is still working.

choices.text: Orders failing with a timeout error
choices.why: Nothing errors; the message simply becomes visible again.

choices.text: Orders moved to the dead-letter queue after 30 seconds
choices.why: A redrive policy counts receives, not seconds, and none is set.

choices.text: Correct behaviour, since SQS extends the timeout for slow consumers automatically
choices.why: It extends nothing unless the consumer asks.

prompt: In the FIFO demonstration, three messages were sent and two had the same deduplication id. How many were received?
What is SNS plus one SQS queue per reader the equivalent of in RabbitMQ?

choices.text: A fanout exchange with a queue bound for each reader
choices.why: Right, and with the same limit: no copy of the past.

choices.text: The default exchange
choices.why: That delivers to one queue, by name.

choices.text: A dead-letter exchange
choices.why: That collects what was given up on.

choices.text: A RabbitMQ stream read from offset zero by every reader
choices.why: That would give replay, which SNS does not.

prompt: Each message asks for a PDF invoice that takes up to two minutes to render. Why does the section lean towards a queue?

choices.text: Kafka cannot carry messages that ask for a PDF
choices.why: It can carry anything; the issue is progress.

choices.text: A slow message holds up one worker, not everything behind it in a partition
choices.why: Right. A queue acknowledges per message.

choices.text: A queue renders PDFs faster
choices.why: The broker renders nothing.

choices.text: Queues keep messages longer than logs do
choices.why: The reverse.

prompt: The warehouse load must rebuild a day's sales after a bug, and the packing team needs one task per shipped sale. What arrangement does the section describe?

choices.text: Sales on a queue, and the warehouse reads the dead letters
choices.why: Dead letters are failures, not a history.

choices.text: Everything on Kafka, with the packers as one consumer group reading the sales topic
choices.why: Possible, but slow tasks then hold up partitions; the section keeps packing on a queue.

choices.text: Everything on RabbitMQ, with a fanout per reader
choices.why: A fanout gives no replay, and the warehouse needs one.

choices.text: Sales on Kafka; a small consumer puts packing tasks on a RabbitMQ queue
choices.why: Right. The log for what happened, the queue for what has to be done.

prompt: Put the life of a message on a RabbitMQ work queue in order.
items: The producer publishes it to an exchange
The exchange routes it into the queue
The server delivers it to one free consumer

prompt: Ponto Final wants every system to be able to rebuild its stock figures from all of last year's sales. Which of the tools this lesson runs serves that?

choices.text: An SQS FIFO queue, because it keeps order
choices.why: Order is kept, but delivered messages are deleted.

choices.text: None: that is a log's job, with retention long enough
choices.why: Right. Replay is the one thing queues give up.

choices.text: SNS, because every subscriber gets a copy
choices.why: Only of what is published after it subscribes.

choices.text: A RabbitMQ queue with a long TTL
choices.why: TTL limits how long a message waits; a read still deletes it.
